items.excerpt: Democrats had a feeling that the midterms would go well for their candidates. But few would have predicted that traditionally red states like Mississippi would flip. Now, Scott Colom will head to Washington as the state’s first Democratic senator since 1982. The House tried and failed to impeach the Defense Secretary Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth this week. Republican Rep. Thomas Massie sponsored a resolution to effectively fire the head of the military. But his fellow GOP members did not back him. And Jensen Huang, the co-founder and now former CEO of Nvidia, resigned on Thursday. That’s after revelations of several affairs with his employees and a potential Chinese spy. And, in global news, President Donald Trump said he would hold off on new military action against Iran after appeals from Gulf allies, but the U.S. military continues to build its presence in the Middle East region. Saudi air defences intercepted Houthi missiles and drones launched towards Riyadh, Mecca, and other regions. Houthis have denied targeting Mecca, saying they only target oil facilities and military bases. And there were two days of U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi. They ended with no major breakthrough. It was the first meeting between the two delegations in nine months.

items.title: Headlines for November 13, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## Sen. Chris Van Hollen Will Challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate Majority Leader Nov 13, 2026 Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen said Thursday he will challenge New York’s Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader when Democrats retake control of both chambers of Congress in January. This follows historic gains for Democrats in last week’s midterm elections. They’ll now control at least 255 seats in the House of Representatives and 55 in the Senate. This is Senator Van Hollen speaking on MS NOW. ... Van Hollen is the first Democratic senator to launch a leadership challenge since 1994. His bid was quickly endorsed by Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Vermont independent Senator Bernie Sanders. ... ## Nvidia’s Colette Kress to Serve as Interim CEO as Jensen Huang Resigns Amid Scandals Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned. The chip maker says its longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will serve as interim CEO while Nvidia’s board of directors searches for a permanent replacement. Huang stepped down as Reuters reported he’d had an intimate relationship with a second employee, whom Reuters did not name. That follows reports that Huang had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence officials claim was spying for Beijing as part of a Chinese intelligence operation seeking to acquire advanced computer chips, which are banned by U.S. export controls. Huang reportedly helped the alleged spy acquire at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips for China via a Singapore-based cloud computing company called Megaspeed International. Meanwhile, Bloomberg reports Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before House lawmakers in a closed-door hearing later this month. Nvidia has lost nearly $2 trillion in market capitalization since its all-time high in early October. We’ll have more on this story after headlines. ## Microsoft Outage Disrupts Communications for Millions Across 74 Countries In more technology news, Microsoft is scrambling to fix a major outage that’s disrupted communication for millions of people across at least 74 countries since Thursday morning. The outage has cut off access to Microsoft’s Outlook, Teams and the AI assistant Copilot. ## Iran Says It Blew Up U.S. Early-Warning Radar as Trump Declares, “We Don’t Need a Deal with Iran” Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it destroyed a U.S. early-warning radar system in Bahrain in retaliation for a U.S. strike on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran. Officials also claimed four attacks on oil tankers in ​the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, following strikes on a pair of supertankers one day earlier. Iran’s attacks came as President Trump on Thursday sidelined Vice President JD Vance as the top U.S. negotiator with Iran. Trump said in a social media post he’d directed Vance to instead focus on fighting what Trump called “corruption and crime” in Democratic-controlled cities and states. Trump wrote, “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” ... ## Russia and Ukraine Continue Deadly Strikes as U.S. ... ## Infant Dies of Hypothermia in Gaza as Calls Grow for Israel to Allow Imports of Winter Supplies In Gaza, a Palestinian infant has died from hypothermia after Israeli attacks left his family displaced and living in a tent in Khan Younis. Kinan Ahmed Raqiq was just 9 months old. His death came as Israel continued to impose severe restrictions on imports of fuel and winter supplies into Gaza. U.N. humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher says 150,000 tents remain stuck in warehouses at Gaza’s borders, even as some 350,000 displaced Palestinians face heavy rain, flooding and plummeting temperatures. On Thursday, a group of 49 nations issued a joint call for Israel to ease restrictions on shelter, fuel, water, sanitation and medical supplies to Gaza.

items.title: PPI inflation report October 2026:
items.excerpt: Wholesale prices increased less than expected in October, but inflation pressures persisted and the Federal Reserve is likely still on target for an interest rate increase soon. The producer price index, which measures the prices domestic producers get for their products before they reach the consumer, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.3% for the month, against the Dow Jones consensus for a 0.4% increase, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. Stripping out food and energy, core PPI posted a 0.3% gain, meeting expectations. On an annual basis, headline PPI accelerated 6.5%, up 0.2 percentage point for the highest annual rate since November 2022. The report comes just a few weeks ahead of the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting, Dec. 8-9. Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase in the central bank's key overnight borrowing rate, with slight odds that the Federal Open Market Committee might opt for a half-point hike. Stock market futures added to gains following the release while Treasury yields were mixed. Earlier this week, the BLS reported that inflation at the cash register was hotter than expected. The headline consumer price index saw a 0.4% increase in October while core was up 0.3%, both 0.1 percentage point higher than expected. Because of the government shutdown in October 2025, the BLS couldn't collect some data and refrained from putting out a 12-month inflation figure for CPI. However, the figures showed that the Fed remains a good distance from its 2% inflation goal. "Today's PPI data – which shows some signs of improving, albeit still too-high – is unlikely to change the Fed's approach in December because the CPI data was already outside their comfort zone," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management. Moreover, policymakers are beginning to worry that inflation generated by the Iran war and higher fuel prices, along with President Donald Trump's tariffs, are beginning to spread through the economy. The Fed generally would look through such price pressures as temporary, but the breadth of inflation could indicate that inflation is becoming more entrenched. "We've had some signs of trouble now for several months in a row," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said in a CNBC interview Friday. "If you look at how broad-based the inflation is, it's not just that we're above the target and have been for some time. It's that in categories that are not driven by oil prices and not driven by tariffs, you're still seeing stalled progress and in some cases going the wrong way." Stripping out food, energy and trade services, PPI saw an increase of 0.5% in October. Goods prices increased 0.5% in October, with more than 60% of that move driven by goods excluding food and energy, which actually saw a 0.1% decrease. On an annual basis, the goods index jumped 10.2%, the biggest 12-month surge since October 2022. Final demand services prices increased 0.2%, most of which was linked to transportation and warehousing services, and within that category a 3.9% gain in truck transportation of freight.

items.title: Bessent, Fed’s Goolsbee divided on role of energy shock in inflation By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday that the Federal Reserve should not hike rates because of inflation driven by an "energy supply shock" tied to the Iran war, comments made to CNBC and promptly contradicted on the network by Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, who said price pressures were building far beyond what could be explained by high oil prices. "I think the Fed should understand that this is an energy supply shock," while the underlying US economy is very strong, Bessent said in an interview on CNBC. "So I think that to hike too much into an energy supply shock when it’s coming down, these are very noisy numbers...You know, the Fed’s supposed to look into the future, not look in the rearview mirror." Shortly afterwards, the network hosted Goolsbee, a regular guest on CNBC’s morning Squawk Box show, who said that inflation was not just due to energy, but had spread to the service sector and areas like medical care that are not usually responsive to the price of oil, and was also elevated through strong demand tied to the AI data center buildout. "I respect the secretary and I am trying to figure out the same thing he is trying to figure out, which is how persistent is this inflation? The tariff inflation and oil price shock were supposed to have gone away by now and it hasn’t," Goolsbee said. "One puzzle is why have those supply shocks been as persistent as they have been. A second thing is if demand is overheating and that is contributing to inflation, that is more worrisome... Services inflation, which is probably not coming from tariffs or oil, is one of the more troubling aspects of the inflation reports we have been getting." While not committing to a rate hike, he said the Fed "has definitely got work to do to continue to reestablish its credibility."

items.title: Data-driven insights from the U.S. Bank Economic Research Group | November 13, 2026
items.excerpt: The last mile gets bumpy The economy is entering a more consequential phase of the inflation fight. The earlier energy shock is fading, but underlying price pressures remain stubborn and have become more broadly distributed across the inflation basket. That leaves the Federal Reserve with more work to do, even as higher borrowing costs increasingly weigh on interest-rate-sensitive parts of the economy. That tension was evident throughout this week’s data: consumer and producer inflation remained too firm for comfort, Fed officials signaled that additional tightening is likely, and existing-home sales fell to their weakest pace since 2010. The question is increasingly not whether higher rates are working, but whether they can cool inflation without putting too much pressure on an otherwise resilient economy. What this means for business: Persistent inflation and further Fed tightening point to borrowing costs staying elevated, keeping pressure on financing and rate-sensitive demand even as the broader economy remains resilient. ... 0.4% October’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) report contained an important warning beneath the headline: core services prices excluding housing rose 0.4%, equivalent to a 4.9% annualized pace. Sometimes called “supercore” CPI inflation, the measure captures categories such as transportation, recreation, and medical services, where price pressures remained firm last month. We estimate those prices are up 3.5% from a year ago and have made little sustained progress since early 2025. ... ## CPI The October CPI report offered less inflationary relief than the slower headline suggested. Consumer prices rose 0.4% month-over-month (MoM), easing from September’s 0.6% increase as the earlier surge in energy prices moderated sharply. Food prices accelerated, however, with both grocery and restaurant prices rising, while shelter costs remained firm and accounted for more than 30% of the overall increase. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics did not publish its usual 12-month headline and core readings because the 2025 government shutdown prevented the collection of most price data last October (our estimate puts headline CPI inflation at roughly 3.9% from a year ago). Beneath the headline, core CPI rose 0.3% MoM for a third consecutive month (an estimated 2.8% from a year ago), underscoring the limited progress in underlying inflation. Shelter inflation eased slightly, but owners’ equivalent rent remained firm, while transportation, recreation, and medical care services also posted notable increases. Core goods inflation cooled, although much of that improvement reflected a drop in used-vehicle prices, leaving goods prices to provide less of the disinflationary offset they typically did before the pandemic. Taken together, October did not signal a broad inflationary surge, but measures of inflation breadth suggest that price increases are becoming more widely distributed across the CPI basket, reinforcing the uneven path back toward 2%. ... The producer-price report offered some relief from September’s surge, but little evidence that pipeline inflation has fully cleared. The PPI (Producer Price Index) for final demand rose 0.3% MoM in October ... Energy prices edged lower and services inflation slowed, but food and core goods prices remained firm, while transportation and warehousing costs rose sharply again, led by another increase in truck-freight charges. Core producer prices (excluding food, energy, and trade services) rose 0.5% for a second consecutive month, leaving that underlying measure 4.9% above a year ago and pointing to continued input-cost pressures for businesses.

items.title: Fed’s Jefferson says he is taking his policy cues from inflation By Reuters
items.excerpt: Nov 13 (Reuters) - Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said on Friday that, with the economy growing and the labor market stabilized, he is taking his policy cues from inflation, a remark that suggests he may support further interest-rate hikes to bring it under control. Jefferson joined the 10-2 majority of Fed policymakers who voted at their October meeting to wait for more data to accumulate before considering a rate hike. "Data received since that meeting have been consistent with economic activity and labor market conditions remaining broadly solid, while inflation readings show persistent price pressures," Jefferson said in remarks prepared for delivery at the University of California, San Diego. "Accordingly, I see the trajectory of inflation as providing the more important signal for determining the appropriate stance of monetary policy." Other Fed policymakers in recent weeks have been explicit that elevated and persistent inflation means they would likely support rate hikes that are bigger or come in quicker succession than the single quarter-point increase the Fed delivered in September. Jefferson gave no such guidance. "Going forward, I believe that further policy adjustments should be determined by carefully examining trends in the data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks," he said.

So far, five senators have publicly said they would back Van Hollen, though he said last night that "over 10" senators have given him an endorsement behind closed doors. Schumer has earned a public endorsement from 14 senators so far, and four senators have said they would not back Schumer but did not name who they were supporting. Sen.-elect Chris Pappas of New Hampshire has said he wants "change" though has not given an endorsement thus far.

items.title: GOP state officials appeal block on 2028 mail voting limits : NPR
items.excerpt: # GOP state officials push to revive Trump's mail voting restrictions for 2028 election November 13, 2026 5:18 PM ET Hansi Lo Wang ... Voting for this year's midterm elections just concluded, but Republican officials in a number of states are already looking to shape how votes are cast in 2028. Twelve GOP state attorneys general are pushing to revive the president's bid for mail-in voting restrictions in time for the 2028 election. On Thursday, they started the process of appealing a September order by U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, one of the two judges who blocked the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out a plan released in response to an executive order by President Trump. The Republican state attorneys general represent Alabama, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota and Texas. It's not clear, however, how long some of these states will continue this case, given that Democrats won up and down the ballot in the midterms. In Texas and Kansas, Democratic candidates are set to take control of their states' attorney general's offices in January. ### The Trump administration's voter roll crusade could continue In September, the Supreme Court refused to pause a similar ruling by U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, who is based in Boston. That order stopped USPS from working on its revised rule for federal ballot mail, but it only applied to this year's midterm elections. Nichols' preliminary injunction blocks USPS from implementing the plan for all federal elections, including the 2028 race. It's not clear if the Trump administration plans to appeal Nichols' ruling by Friday's deadline for filing a court notice. Asked about the Justice Department's plans, DOJ spokesperson Matthew Tragesser replied in an email that the department doesn't comment on ongoing litigation. The blocked rule — which the Postal Service released in late August — would require states to turn over lists of voters' names and addresses in order to have them delivered by USPS. ### Tens of millions cast ballots for midterms despite worries of Trump's interference Nichols, a Washington, D.C.-based judge who was nominated by Trump, found that the mailing agency likely has no power to impose that requirement on states. "As the Government concedes, the Postal Service could issue (and enforce) the Rule only if Congress gave it the authority to do so, but here no statute grants the Postal Service the power to issue key parts of the Rule," Nichols wrote. The administration's earlier push to put these new restrictions in place for the midterms alarmed many election officials, who were concerned about last-minute changes causing major disruptions to the tens of millions who regularly vote by mail. Some voters with disabilities and those in places without polling sites, they feared, could have lost the ability to exercise their right to cast a ballot. A whistleblower report claimed the online system officials would need to use to follow USPS' revised ballot requirements had not been properly tested and could have resulted in many eligible voters not getting their mail-in ballots in time or at all. While the Supreme Court ultimately stopped implementation of the USPS rule for the midterms, Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented from that ruling. Fellow conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh said in a concurring opinion that he believed state and local election officials did not have enough time to "reasonably implement the rule" this time. But Kavanaugh noted that "there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority."

items.excerpt: After 8 nominations without a win, Glenn Close is 'overwhelmed' by honorary Oscar Glenn Close is receiving an honorary Oscar on Sunday at the Governors Awards. The 79-year-old actor has been nominated for eight competitive acting Oscars but never won. It's a distinction shared only by Peter O'Toole. Close tells The Associated Press that her first thought was that she didn't need a consolation prize. But Close has come to appreciate the unique opportunity that the honorary Oscar presents. At the untelevised ceremony where there are no “losers,” she and her friends and collaborators have the time to reflect on her body of work as a whole. UK police launch sex offense investigation into children’s author and comedian David Walliams LONDON (AP) — London police say they are investigating children’s author and comedian David Walliams for serious sexual offenses after news outlets reported allegations of misconduct. The Metropolitan Police said it had received a number of allegations of abuse in the past after a joint investigation by ITV News and the Guardian newspaper. The allegations are different from those reported by the news outlets, police said. But they will also look into the news stories to see if there is evidence of other crimes. Hartman follows in the footsteps of other NFL players who have starred on the show. This move breaks from the usual casting of past contestants. The parade will feature a record-breaking 100 inflatables, including Bluey, Mickey Mouse and Hello Kitty. It kicks off at 8:30 a.m. on Thanksgiving in all time zones. A tribute to Dolly Parton, led by Megan Hilty, and special appearances by Melissa Joan Hart and others are planned. NBC and Peacock will broadcast the event, with a Spanish-language simulcast on Telemundo. New balloons and floats will join iconic characters from past parades. ... She also opened the Thursday night show. Juanes won the first award for best pop/rock album. Performers at this year’s bash included Karol G, Anitta, Jorge Drexler and Silvana Estrada. The 2026 Latin Grammy Awards’ person of the year was Daddy Yankee. He became the first Latin urbano artist to receive the honor. He ripped through his biggest hits an hour into the evening, treating the award show stage like a stadium floor. Edgar Barrera became the most awarded person in the show’s history with 30 career wins.
